generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, an effective search is a process, not a single lookup. You plan what you are after, choose keywords such as 'warm-up' and 'injury', search a tool such as your library discovery service or a database, weigh which sources are suitable, and follow references to reach further work. A coach might judge a session-plan study differently from how a sport scientist reads lab data, but the stages are the same. At this stage the point is to see the whole shape of a good search; weighing sources and extending a search are skills that later modules build in full.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students are asked to find sources on the same topic for a seminar on session design.

Tom opens the library search tool, types the topic in, and uses the first article on the list. The job feels done. But Tom skipped almost every stage: no plan, no thought about keywords, no weighing of the study, and no second look. It was one lookup, and whatever came first. This is a one-off lookup, not an effective search.

Amara first sets an objective and picks keywords, then searches the tool, glances over the results to judge which studies look suitable, and follows a reference from the best one to a further source. Her search for evidence on warm-up design moved through the stages in order. This is an effective, planned search.

Both students searched the same tool. Only Amara worked through the stages that make a search effective.
generatedProse.summary: An effective search in the School of Sport is a planned process with stages: plan, identify keywords, use your discovery service, evaluate the sources you find, and extend the search. Whether you coach, test athletes or run programmes, you can now describe these stages and recognise effective searching as a process rather than a one-off lookup. The next lesson takes the first two stages, planning and keywords, and shows you how to do them yourself.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's search effective rather than a one-off lookup?

items.text: She worked through the stages: planned, chose keywords, searched, weighed and extended.
She used the library tool instead of a search engine.
She used the very first article the search returned.
She finished the task in a single step.

feedback.correct: That's right. Moving through the stages in order is what makes a search effective.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID across the search, not which tool she opened.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's search was effective because she worked through the stages. Using the tool, taking the first result, or finishing in one step are not what made the difference.
